The eleven ratings for TKH Group
TKH Group (TWEKA-NL) · Investment memo · 24 October 2026

TKH Group: the market has paid for the break-up but not for the net-cash automation company that follows it, and the best entry point is likely to come during the 2027 re-basing window

Written on 24 October 2026 at a share price of €50.25. The Q3 trading update of about 10 November 2026 is the first test of everything below. Money is in euros. EPS is on the model's basis (before amortisation of acquired intangibles) unless the company's adjusted basis is named; the company's basis runs about €0.30 to €0.35 a share lower. Sources and conventions are in the end notes.

The case in brief. TKH, a €2.0 billion Dutch group, is selling its weaker 40% to keep its stronger 60%. The part being sold is Electrification (subsea and grid cables), which earns an 8% EBITA margin and ties up 25.6% of sales in working capital. The part that stays is Automation (machine vision, and tyre-building machinery under the VMI brand), which earns an 18.4% margin, ties up 12.4% of sales in working capital and earns a 27% pro forma return on capital employed (ROCE).

The transaction is dated and backed by shareholders. Shareholders approved the sale on 3 September 2026, TKH targets a signing by Q1 2027, and an external chief executive, Guido Grandi, takes over on 1 January 2027. The sale proceeds of about €950 million (including the fibre business) equal nearly half of the market capitalisation and turn net debt of 1.8x EBITDA into net cash. The model's base case returns €600 million of that cash through buybacks over 2027 to 2030.

On the model's forecasts the shares are worth €75.94 by December 2027 at Viewforth's guideline multiple of 16.41x two-year-forward earnings. That value is a 51% gain on today's €50.25, with about €3.20 of declared dividends (6%) on top.

The five things Richard needs to hold in his head.

1

The market has paid for the break-up event but not for the company that remains afterwards. The shares are up 35% in a year, trade at the 84th percentile of their five-year forward multiple, and carry a Buy rating from all five covering brokers. The market owns a break-up with a date. The market has not priced five things, in either direction:

  • The sale price. No broker has a number except Jefferies, whose two figures (€0.8 billion and €1.28 billion) contradict each other.
  • The standalone Automation margin after central costs. The margin is about 16%, not the 17% to 19% headline target.
  • The FY2027 earnings trough on the continuing perimeter. EPS falls to about €2.45, down 30%.
  • The dividend arithmetic. The FY2027 consensus dividend of €1.98 is unreachable on continuing earnings.
  • The size of the capital return. Only one broker models any buyback.

The gap between Viewforth's view and the market's is almost entirely about this second half of the thesis.

2

The next six months carry the negatives and the following twelve months carry the positives. Between February and June 2027 the market will receive four negatives in one window. A new chief executive will reset the earnings base with €20 to €40 million of one-off costs. The Automation margin target will probably be restated to a company basis that includes central costs. The dividend of €1.60 will fall short of the €1.70 consensus. The IFRS 5 re-basing (the accounting move of Electrification into discontinued operations) will make the FactSet consensus series show a 35% to 45% cut in revenue and EPS while the value of the company does not change. After that window come the closing, the proceeds, a capital-return framework, the first standalone half-year (August 2027) and, if tyre makers restart capital spending late in 2027, the Machinery recovery in FY2028 and FY2029. An investor who buys now is paid to hold through the window, but the best entry point of the next 18 months is likely to be inside the window, when the screens say estimates have been cut by 40%.

3

A transaction, not management, delivers most of the improvement. Group EBITA margin rises by roughly 7 points from 10.8% in FY2025 to 18.3% in FY2029. About 4.5 points of that rise come from the change of perimeter, 1.5 points from absorption at the Eemshaven cable plant (already in FY2026), and 1 point from management action. EPS grows by €2.50 from the FY2027 trough to FY2030; about 37% of that growth comes from the lower share count, 28% from the Machinery cycle, 25% from Vision and 10% from central costs and interest. The case is therefore robust to management error, because the two businesses that remain have held 15% to 21% margins through a customer destock and a capital-spending freeze. The case is fragile to two things outside management's control: the price a buyer pays when acquisition financing is expensive, and the timing of orders from Michelin, Goodyear, Bridgestone, Continental and Pirelli.

4

On continuing earnings the market already pays about 14x FY2028 EPS. The share price of €50.25 is 14.3x the model's FY2028 EPS of €3.51. That multiple sits inside the stock's ten-year "defendable" band (75th percentile 14.4x), not at the 12.6x that the consensus-based screens show. The re-rating that the sum-of-the-parts valuations promise (Jefferies values the parts at €103.5 a share) is therefore partly a re-labelling of earnings the market is already paying for. The genuine upside is EPS compounding at about 25% a year from the FY2027 trough through FY2030, on a net-cash balance sheet, with the share count falling by a fifth. The multiple amplifies the return; earnings growth drives it.

5

The skew is positive on earnings, roughly symmetric on the share price, and the gains come late. Three points support the earnings skew. FY2026 guidance ("organic growth") is a floor that TKH should beat by about 30% on EBITA. The two largest uncertain items in the four-year numbers, the buyback and the tyre makers' replacement wave, are more likely to happen than not and appear in no published forecast. If the sale slips, FY2027 and FY2028 EPS are higher than in the base case, not lower. Against that, there is a 25% probability of a 25% to 30% drawdown to €36 to €40 if the sale slips into late 2027 and Machinery order intake stays below €60 million a quarter.

Where Viewforth differs from the market. First, the sell-side's valuation anchor for Electrification is too high: Jefferies uses 12.2x EBITDA, against Nexans at 7x and a 20% de-rating of cable-sector shares since June. Second, the FY2027 consolidated consensus is achievable but has the wrong composition: brokers carry €37 million of financial charges against Viewforth's €26 million and a Machinery line 8% above Viewforth's. Third, nobody has published continuing-perimeter numbers, so the first re-based consensus will start below where the business will land.

Where Viewforth agrees with the market. FY2026 is beatable, Eemshaven is repaired, Vision's restocking demand is real but partly a refill of customer inventory, and the Machinery trough is real but nobody can date its end.

Bottom line. For the next two reporting periods TKH is a cyclical recovery plus a corporate event; after that it becomes a focused automation company with a cash pile. The event is well-founded, dated, and about two-thirds likely to close by mid-2027. The money is in the aftermath, where no published forecast yet exists. This memo changes no forecast input: the model's base case (a sale at 7x EBITDA, €600 million of buybacks starting in H2 2027, and Machinery orders turning late in 2027) is where Viewforth's own judgement sits. The model's FY2029 and FY2030 EPS are read as the upper edge of the range, because the model's buyback mechanic retires shares at today's price rather than at the higher future price.

Scorecard: the twelve topics

The five judgements that move the value most, and their arithmetic

Five judgements move the value of the shares most over the next one to two years. For each one, the table and the paragraphs below show what happens to the numbers if the judgement is wrong by a plausible amount. The base is the model's FY2028 EPS of €3.51 on about 34 million average shares and FY2029 EPS of €4.43 on about 31 million average shares.

Judgement 1: Electrification sells at about 7x FY2027 EBITDA, for an enterprise value of €850 million and net proceeds of €830 million. Each 1x of multiple on the unit's roughly €125 million of FY2027 EBITDA is worth €125 million of proceeds. Spent on buybacks at about €62 a share, €125 million retires 2.0 million shares, about 6% of the FY2029 share count, and so adds about 6% (€0.27) to FY2029 EPS.

  • Upside case, 9x: the multiple sits between Prysmian's Atkore and Encore deal multiples (8.2x and 9.8x) and NKT's 10x. Proceeds rise by €250 million, 4.0 million more shares are retired, and FY2029 EPS reaches about €4.95 (plus 12%).
  • Downside case, 5.5x: a stock-market listing at Nexans' multiple, with a discount for Eemshaven's two-quarter operating record (a concern the Dutch shareholders' association, VEB, raised at the annual general meeting). Proceeds fall by €190 million and FY2029 EPS falls to about €4.05 (minus 9%).

The asymmetry lies in the narrative rather than the arithmetic. A sale at Viewforth's base price would disappoint against the loudest published sum of the parts (Jefferies' €1.28 billion for Electrification) while still confirming the strategy.

Judgement 2: Tyre makers' order intake turns late in 2027, so Machinery revenue rises 8% in FY2028 to €465 million at a 16.0% margin (€74 million of EBITA). The transmission chain is slow. A Tier 1 tyre maker's capital-spending decision becomes an order for VMI two to four quarters later; an order becomes revenue over 10 to 12 months; and extra revenue drops through to profit at about 28%.

  • If the freeze runs through 2028 (intake near €50 million a quarter): FY2028 revenue falls to about €400 million at a 14% margin. The 14% margin is a floor, because the segment held 16% through a 38% decline in its order backlog. EBITA falls to €56 million, €18 million below the base; after tax at 24% the loss is €14 million, or €0.41 a share on 34 million shares (minus 12% of FY2028 EPS).
  • If intake turns early in 2027 (the path in the research file's second forecast set): revenue reaches €484 million at 16.5%, adding €5.5 million of EBITA and €0.12 of EPS (plus 3.5%).

FY2028 therefore carries more downside than upside from Machinery. FY2029 carries the reverse, because a deferred replacement wave is larger when it finally comes.

Judgement 3: Central costs fall from €25 million to €18 million in FY2028 and to €15 million from FY2029, and the new chief executive does not cut the earnings base further. Every precedent has the stranded cost arriving before the saving: Aalberts' holding costs rose to €25 to €35 million in its divestment year, Sandvik suffered 100 to 200 basis points of dis-synergy, and DSM-Firmenich carried CHF 75 million of stranded cost.

  • If stranded costs hold at €30 million through FY2028: EBITA falls by €12 million, net profit by €9 million, and EPS by €0.27 (minus 8%).
  • If Grandi cuts the share of research spending that TKH capitalises from 51.6% toward Basler's 28.6%: about €20 million moves into operating cost, net profit falls by €15 million and EPS by €0.45 (minus 13%). Cash is unaffected, but the earnings base to which the multiple applies is lower.
  • Both together: FY2028 EPS falls to about €2.80, and the market would hear a "reset" story that is wrong in substance but right in appearance.

Judgement 4: TKH returns the proceeds through €600 million of buybacks over FY2027 to FY2030 rather than spending them on acquisitions. Three facts support the judgement: the July 2026 shareholder circular commits excess cash to buybacks and dividends while leverage stays within 2.0x; on the net-cash arithmetic there is nowhere else for the money to go; and HAL Trust (holder of 10.23%) and the minority shareholders at the annual general meeting have asked for a return. Three facts argue against it: management lists buybacks last among its uses of cash, Grandi's plan for Norma's disposal proceeds was reinvestment, and only one broker models a buyback.

  • Partial diversion: each €200 million spent on vision software companies at 15x EBITDA, rather than on TKH shares at 12x earnings, costs about 4% of EPS. Diverting €300 million costs 6% (€0.27 of FY2029 EPS).
  • No buyback at all (the cash sits on the balance sheet): FY2029 EPS falls to about €3.85 (minus 13%), and the capital-allocation feedback loop that justifies the Reinforcing lifecycle phase never starts.

Judgement 5: The two-year-forward P/E multiple reaches the guideline 16.41x by December 2027. The model carries about €4.60 of two-year-forward EPS at that date, so each 1x of multiple is worth €4.60 a share, or 9% of today's price. At 12.6x (today's consensus-based multiple, unchanged) the December 2027 value is about €58, a 16% gain before dividends. At 14.4x (the ten-year 75th percentile) the value is about €66 (plus 32%). At 16.41x the value is €75.94 (plus 51%). The multiple is the largest single swing item in the 18-month return and the item least within anyone's control, because it depends on the market seeing standalone numbers that it has never seen before.

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

Key message. TKH's external tailwinds are strong and measurable in its order books, but two of the three structural tailwinds belong to the cable business being sold. The one material headwind, the tyre makers' capital-spending freeze, sits in the highest-return business that stays.

Evidence: the tailwinds. Three structural tailwinds and one cyclical tailwind show up in the order books, not just in the narrative.

  • Dutch grid (structural, sold with Electrification). Dutch distribution grid operators plan €10.8 billion of capital spending to 2030, against €5.9 billion in 2025. The government has made grid expansion a national priority, with a 120GW connection backlog and 15,000 customers waiting. TKH holds €1.4 billion of signed framework contracts outside the reported order book, including the eight-year, €650 million Alliander contract from mid-2026. Onshore cable turnover rose 26.4% in H1 2026, with the plants near full capacity.
  • Offshore inter-array cables (structural, sold with Electrification). European demand for the cables that connect turbines within a wind farm is projected to rise six-fold by 2030, and the tender pipeline covers 14,400 kilometres across 92 projects. TKH has won over 80% of the European tenders it entered in 2024 to 2026, because the three export-cable majors are booked with 525kV work into 2028 and beyond. Offshore turnover rose 81.6% organically in H1 2026, because supply, not demand, had been the constraint.
  • Machine vision (cyclical upturn, stays with TKH). The Vision order book rose to €170.1 million at June 2026 from €125.8 million at December 2025, led by Asia-Pacific semiconductor and electronics customers. Peers confirm the upturn: Jenoptik raised its FY2026 EBITDA margin guidance to about 22% on 21 October after Q3 orders rose 24%; Basler's H1 order intake rose 59%; Cognex guided Q3 revenue up 23%; and the Eurozone manufacturing purchasing managers' index reached 52.9 in September, its highest since May 2022.
  • Fibre (structural, sold). Demand from AI data centres has made the fibre business profitable (€10.7 million of H1 2026 EBITA), which makes the fibre business easier to sell.

Evidence: the headwinds. The headwinds are specific and dated.

  • Tyre-building machinery. The Machinery order book fell 38% year on year to €259.2 million at June 2026, because Tier 1 tyre makers deferred plant decisions on tariffs, energy costs and permitting. Michelin is holding 2026 capital spending at about €2 billion with volumes down; Goodyear cut 2026 capital spending to $725 million from $1.19 billion and is closing its Fayetteville plant by end-2027. Morgan Stanley's machine-tool down-cycle has now run 39 months, against 13 to 14 months after 2008 and 2020.
  • Interest rates and risk appetite. The US ten-year yield is near 5.1%, and the market refuses re-ratings and penalises leverage. That regime hurts the transaction (an initial public offering window, and leveraged buyers' financing) more than the operations.
  • Cable-peer valuations. The share prices of cable peers, which set Electrification's sale price, are down 20% from their June peaks.
  • Input costs. Copper is up 30% and European power and gas prices are up 97% and 133% year on year. Cable contracts pass copper costs through with a lag, so copper inflates working capital rather than cutting margin. Energy is the one real cost headwind.

Inference. About 40% of revenue now rests on structural demand with more than two years of visibility, 30% on a cyclical upturn with four months of order cover, and 25% on a cyclical trough with no confirmed turn. Eighteen months ago the mix was the reverse. The composition matters more than the direction: the two structural tailwinds sit in the business being sold, so they support the sale price rather than the earnings that TKH's shareholders will own. The cyclical headwind sits in the highest-return business that stays.

So what. For consolidated FY2026 and a consolidated FY2027, the external environment nets to a tailwind worth several points of organic growth above TKH's normal low-to-mid single-digit rate (H1 2026 organic growth was 14%, and Q2 alone 18%). For the standalone Automation business from mid-2027, the environment nets to roughly neutral until tyre makers' capital spending turns, because industry digests expect the Vision restocking to fade toward mid-single-digit growth by Q4 2026.

Strongest counter-case. The cable scarcity window closes in 2027 to 2028, as about 30% more top-tier capacity arrives: NKT's Karlskrona expansion commissions in Q2 2027, Nexans' Charleroi plant in mid-2027, and Sumitomo's Scottish plant opened on 19 October 2026. Offshore wind developers' financing problems are already delaying cable call-offs: TenneT's July report moved some offshore investment into 2027, Vattenfall pushed Zeevonk's first commercial operation to 2029, and Fugro's offshore wind backlog fell 47%. A buyer of Electrification will price both risks. In addition, the Vision restocking is partly a refill of customer inventory, and the Rothschild Redburn short-cycle indicator fell 6% quarter on quarter in Q3.

What would change my view. Upward: a Machinery order book above €259 million in November, or Tier 1 tyre makers' 2027 capital-spending guidance in February 2027 that rises; Europe joining Asia-Pacific in lifting the Vision order book. Downward: a 2027 offshore call-off slipping out of Eemshaven's 600-kilometre production plan; Chinese 2D vision pricing (at 50% to 67% discounts) showing up in Vision's 62.7% added-value margin.

Market versus me. The market reads the tailwinds as TKH's. Viewforth reads them as mostly the buyer's from mid-2027, and reads the tyre-machinery headwind as the factor that sets the FY2028 number. The market and Viewforth agree on the direction of the forces and disagree on who will own them.

Score: 62. Strong, well-evidenced tailwinds in grid, offshore and vision put TKH above the European median, held back because two of the three attach to the asset being sold and the one cyclical headwind sits in the business that stays.

#2 Internally-driven corporate change, and the absence of problems

Key message. TKH is undergoing the most complete corporate reset in its listed history, and almost every dated step since September 2025 has happened on time. What remains is the transaction itself and the use of its proceeds.

The sale route and the people. TKH is running a dual-track process, a trade sale or a stock-market listing, targeted at Q4 2026 or Q1 2027. Guido Grandi is the first external chief executive in four decades and brings a turnaround record (Norma, WKW); the 25-year incumbent chief executive moves to run Electrification.

The targets. TKH set standalone Electrification targets in August 2026 (revenue growth over 9%, EBITDA margin over 19%) to support the sale price. TKH set the 2028 Automation targets (5% to 7% growth, 17% to 19% EBITA margin, 25% to 30% ROCE) in September 2025, below the prior ambitions, and the Automation segments already meet those targets at the segment level.

Inference. The reset removes the two things that made the group hard to model: a capital-intensive project business with penalty risk (€11.6 million of late-delivery penalties and €15 million of start-up losses in 2025) and a chief executive without a successor. The reset also fits the sector's rule that a break-up re-rates the parent when what leaves is worse than what stays. Beatable targets set in September 2025 plus a new chief executive are the classic set-up for two years of guidance upgrades, once the new chief executive has reset the base.

So what. The internal forces justify a base case in which TKH beats FY2026 consensus and meets a consolidated FY2027 consensus. The main uncertainty is the shape of the group after separation, not the operating trajectory. Two things could spoil the base case: a delayed or low-priced transaction, and stranded costs that make the remaining company less profitable than the segment numbers imply.

Problems present today

  • Trade working capital at 18.3% of turnover against a 12% to 15% target, flattered by €35.5 million of reverse factoring and €43.8 million of non-recourse factoring
  • H1 2026 cash conversion of only 15% of EBITDA
  • 51.6% of research spending capitalised, in the top 5% of peers
  • The new auditor's key audit matter on revenue recognised over time
  • The Alphatronics disposal gain reported at €0.9 million in March and €2.8 million in August, without a reconciliation

Problems that are plausible

  • Friction between two chief executives from September 2026 until closing (Grandi left Norma over strategic differences)
  • A "kitchen-sink" write-down by Grandi at the FY2026 results
  • Separation costs above €15 million, and tax leakage on the carve-out (the Dutch participation exemption applies to a share sale; no tax ruling has been disclosed)
  • Dis-synergies that the company has not quantified

Governance travels with the new company. A trust office foundation (STAK) votes the shares behind the listed depositary receipts, exchanging receipts for voting shares is capped at 1% of capital, a continuity foundation can issue preference shares up to 50% of capital, and EPS is absent from management's incentive metrics.

Strongest counter-case. Everything hinges on a single transaction whose price, structure and timing are unknown, in a financing environment that has worsened since the extraordinary general meeting. The people delivering the transaction have a poor three-year record (two guidance misses, of 13% and 20%, and a plant two years late) and a good twelve-month record. The capital-allocation record is one €25 million buyback in 2022 and nothing after the Dewetron proceeds arrived.

What would change my view. Upward: a signing announcement with a named buyer and a price above €0.9 billion; a capital-allocation framework at the March 2027 results. Downward: the November update dropping "on schedule" from the separation language; an extension of the restricted period past Q1 2027.

Market versus me. The market credits the break-up fully and the capital return hardly at all (only Jefferies models one). Viewforth carries €600 million of buybacks in the base case, but starting in H2 2027, later than the research file's second forecast set assumed. The reason is precedent: external chief executives at family-influenced Dutch companies have taken about fifteen months to present a strategy.

Score: 72. A shareholder-approved separation with a target quarter, an external chief executive with a start date, reset targets, completed capex and an authorised buyback put TKH in the top quartile of European companies on corporate change, with the deduction for a single-transaction dependency and an unproven allocator.

#3 Value chain, business model, financial profile, management

Key message. TKH keeps one fortress (VMI tyre-building machinery) and one contested specialist position (machine vision), and sells two time-limited cable advantages. The financial profile is improving from a weak base, and management is the weakest element and the one changing most.

Industry structure and competitive advantage

VMI is a fortress. VMI holds over 70% of the market for outsourced radial tyre-building machines and 30% to 35% of the installed base. VMI's moat rests on 1,400 active patents and on customer approval cycles for new machines that take years. The Tier 1 tyre makers' share of VMI's intake rose from 10% to 55% in a decade, and VMI lost no order to a competitor during the 38% backlog decline. UNIXX, the only autonomous tyre-building platform, sells at two to three times the price of a MAXX machine (€10 to €12 million a system) and is moving to repeat orders and a motorcycle-tyre variant.

Long-run demand favours VMI. Replacement accounts for 75% to 80% of machine demand, over 40% of non-TKH machines are older than 20 years, Tier 1 tyre makers are slowly outsourcing more than their current 50%, and the number of tyre variants has quadrupled in ten years. Chinese machine builders (such as Mesnac, which has a plant in León, Mexico) compete for Tier 2 and Tier 3 tyre makers, where VMI's moat is thinner.

Machine vision is a contested specialist position. LMI is the number one in 3D inline inspection (about 12% share), with real switching costs for customers. 2D vision is commoditising under pressure from Hikrobot and Dahua, from software-only entrants and from robot makers that buy sensors directly from chip vendors. TKH spends 5% of group sales (over 10% of Vision sales) on research, against 13% to 14% at Cognex and Basler.

The cable advantages are real but time-limited, and they leave with Electrification. Dry-design inter-array cable, winter certification, 132kV capability and the Dutch framework contracts last only as long as the scarcity window and the framework terms.

Group scale is a cost, not an advantage. The unallocated head office costs about €25 million a year, and the sell-side puts the conglomerate discount at 46% to 50%.

Financial profile: recovering, geared and cash-poor, with a high-quality core

Group adjusted EBITA margin has stayed between 10% and 13% for a decade: 10.8% in FY2025, 11.9% in H1 2026 and 13.3% in Q2 2026. By segment in H1 2026, Vision earned 20.2%, Machinery 16.0%, Electrification 8.0% and Other 7.4%. Group ROCE was 13.8% in FY2025, made up of 2.6% pre-tax in Electrification and 27.4% pro forma in Automation. Free cash flow was negative in two of the last five years (minus €93 million in FY2023 on FactSet's definition) and only 0.7x net income in FY2025. Covenant net debt was €502 million at June 2026 (1.8x EBITDA), or €597 million including leases.

Against the four peers in the research file (thyssenkrupp, Prysmian, Nexans, Jenoptik), TKH's consensus EBITDA margin path (16%, 17%, 18%) sits below Jenoptik's (22% to 24%) and above the cable makers', with the weakest cash conversion in the set.

Four corrections the reported earnings base needs before it can be trustedWhy
1. Strip one-off itemsA €35.8 million untaxed disposal gain made up 38% of FY2025 reported profit
2. Adjust for capitalised development51.6% of research spending is capitalised, far above peers
3. Normalise the tax rateUse 24%
4. Account for the two amortisation linesAbout €55 million a year sits between adjusted EBITA and adjusted net profit

Management, strategy and culture: the weakest element, and the one most in flux

The outgoing team ran a strong niche business well and a capital-intensive business badly. The team invested €200 million in Electrification capacity that earns 2.6% before deciding to sell it, never brought working capital to target after 2021, lowered the Accelerate 2025 targets rather than meeting them, and extended the chief executive's contract past retirement without a successor. The team's last twelve months were its best.

The strategy is sensible but late, rather than bold. The strategy concentrates capital where returns are highest and sells the asset-heavy unit at the point its value has been repaired. The strategy does not explain how a €1 billion automation group spending 5% of sales on research widens its moat against Keyence, Cognex and Chinese entrants. The strategy's growth leg relies on bolt-on vision acquisitions, which is where TKH's integration record is worst (seven acquisitions, with sister brands competing for the same customers) and where management itself says prices are inflated.

The incoming chief executive is a turnaround operator with no TKH record. Grandi spent twenty months at Norma, holding a steady 8% margin through a 5.5% revenue decline, and left over the pace of a divestment.

The culture is decentralised and entrepreneurial in the operating companies (customer satisfaction scores 8.6) and family-centralised at the top. The break-up is itself an admission that the group structure did not work.

Inference and so-what. Model the post-separation group as two businesses, not one. Machinery has market-leader economics (16% to 20% margins through the cycle), with volume as the only variable. Vision has specialist economics (17% to 21% margins), with its margin dependent on holding the software share of sales against commoditisation. Assume outstanding execution in Machinery and ordinary execution elsewhere. Treat guidance from the current team as a floor to be beaten, and expect Grandi to reset the earnings base and the Automation targets during 2027. Treat capital allocation as the largest unresolved management decision.

Strongest counter-case. A standalone €1 billion automation company that spends 5% of sales on research, has a STAK structure that blocks takeover and activist discipline, and is run by a chief executive the market has not met, is a medium-quality business being asked to earn a high-quality multiple.

What would change my view. Upward: disclosed software-licence revenue; Allied Vision's direct-sales push keeping the distributor channel intact (39% of vision sales go through distributors, and a JAI expert describes "serious channel conflicts"); a Grandi team announcement with external hires. Downward: a large vision acquisition at 15x EBITDA or more before the buyback starts.

Market versus me. The market's narrative treats Automation as a single "asset-light technology business" that deserves Jefferies' 16.6x and 14.5x EV/EBITDA multiples. Viewforth sees a fortress plus a contested specialist, worth those multiples only once TKH demonstrates its software share of sales and a stable sales channel.

Score: 52. A genuine fortress in tyre-building machinery and a defensible 3D niche are offset by a commoditising 2D business, a decade of 10% to 13% group margins and poor cash conversion, and a management team that is the weakest element and is changing; mid-table in Europe, improving by construction.

#4 Conservative guidance, conservative expectations, and the record of delivery

Key message. FY2026 guidance is a floor that TKH will beat, but FY2027 consensus has no cushion. Expect the pattern "beat, reset, beat": a beat in March 2027, a reset of the base by the new chief executive in the same announcement, and beats against the reset base through 2027 and 2028.

FY2026 guidance is a floor. FY2026 guidance is qualitative: "organic growth in turnover and adjusted EBITA". TKH reiterated that guidance on 11 August even though H1 adjusted EBITA beat consensus by 11% and grew 43.5% organically, and cited the restrictions of the dual-track sale process as the reason for not giving a number. The model's FY2026 adjusted EBITA of €248 million is 31% above FY2025. Consensus (five brokers; FactSet median EPS €3.10 and EBITDA €302 million) sits far above the guidance, so the market already understands the conservatism: Jefferies calls the guidance sandbagging, and ING calls it excessive conservatism.

FY2027 consensus has no cushion. The FY2027 consensus EPS of €3.71 equals the sum of management's segment targets on the consolidated perimeter. Consensus therefore requires Electrification to move toward its 17% to 19% EBITDA margin target and Machinery to stop falling. The model's consolidated FY2027 EPS also lands at €3.71, but with a different composition: Electrification at a 17% EBITDA margin, Machinery 8% below consensus, and financial charges of €26 million against the roughly €37 million brokers carry. The consensus figure holds only if the two items least within management's control offset each other.

TKH's record depends on the type of task. In product businesses during an upturn and without a capital project, TKH beats: in FY2021 and FY2022, and in Q1 and H1 2026. During plant ramp-ups and customer destocks, TKH misses by 13% to 20%. The files show no in-year numerical upgrade. TKH's behaviour has flipped from over-promising to under-promising, which is not yet the pattern of a company that reliably tracks its guidance. The August 2026 raise of the Electrification standalone target was partly a change of basis: a 19% EBITDA margin equals about 14% to 14.5% EBITA, the top of the old 12% to 15% EBITA range.

Inference. On the operating side, the next 18 months are the kind of task TKH does well: no plant ramp, capital spending at the level of depreciation, Vision in an upturn, and Electrification absorbing an already-built plant. On the corporate side the task is new. The pattern to expect is "beat, reset, beat". The FY2026 floor will be beaten in March 2027; the new chief executive, who has every incentive to set a low first guide, will reset the base in the same announcement; and TKH will then beat the reset base through 2027 and 2028. The probabilities are in the chart below. The 50% probability that the 2028 Automation margin target is restated from 17% to 19% to about 15% to 17% on a company basis matters most, because the market will call that restatement a cut.

So what. Expectations are conservative for FY2026 but only fair for a consolidated FY2027, so the cushion implied by the "sandbagging" headline does not extend into FY2027. The real conservatism will appear after the reset, on the continuing perimeter. If the new chief executive's first guide is set below the model's FY2027 continuing EBITA of €163 million, the guide leaves room for upgrades at the H1 2027 results (about 45% probability of a raise, 40% of a hold and 15% of a cut).

Strongest counter-case. TKH turned "conservative and closed" (ING's phrase) after repeated misses, guides qualitatively because the sale process requires it, reports order books only at half-years, and from January will be run by a chief executive who has never given a TKH guide. Such a company is not demonstrating conservatism as a policy; it is demonstrating a regulatory restriction and the absence of a record.

What would change my view. Upward: a sharpened guide ("strong growth") in November; a numerical FY2027 frame for the continuing business in March, including a central-cost figure. Downward: a Q3 update that does not reiterate guidance.

Market versus me. The market reads FY2026 as sandbagged and FY2027 as comfortable. Viewforth reads FY2026 as a floor the market already prices, and FY2027 as achievable but with no cushion and the wrong composition. Viewforth also expects the market to read the March 2027 reset as a cut even though the substance is unchanged.

Score: 55. Guidance is a floor and the twelve-month record is good, which lifts TKH above the median, but the three-year record is poor, the record of raising guidance is absent, and the chief executive who will own the next three years has none; a company rebuilding credibility, not one that has earned it.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops

Key message. TKH's profits react strongly to revenue, but the biggest fixed-cost lever leaves with the cable business. The shareholder keeps a moderately levered product business plus a large balance-sheet swing.

Operating leverage is high, works in both directions, and is currently favourable. The company's own sensitivities show that a 1% change in turnover moves adjusted EBITA by €8.9 million with costs fixed (a drop-through of about 50%, consistent with the 50% added-value margin), and that a 1% change in gross margin moves adjusted EBITA by €17.6 million. A 5% change in group revenue therefore moves EBITA by roughly €45 million. The record confirms the leverage in both directions: from FY2021 to FY2022 revenue rose 19% and EBIT 31%; from FY2023 to FY2024 revenue fell 7% and EBIT 21%; in H1 2026 revenue rose 11.4% and adjusted EBITA 41.7%. Personnel costs grew only 3.3% in H1 2026 against revenue growth of 11.4%, which explains the whole H1 beat.

SegmentType of leverageEvidence
Electrification (sold)Plant absorption: high fixed costsEemshaven ran at about half of its 1,200-kilometre capacity in 2026, with depreciation at 4.6% of sales and a largely fixed labour and energy base. Absorption delivered almost all of the €26 million H1 EBITA improvement. An H2 2026 EBITA margin of 12%, against 8% in H1, adds about €15 million on its own.
Vision (stays)Drop-through of 35% to 45%Organic EBITA grew 27.5% on revenue growth of 12.1% in H1 2026.
Machinery (stays)Flexible costs, modest drop-through of about 28%18% of turnover is aftermarket and service, and components are outsourced. The margin held at 16% on falling volume, so upside drop-through is correspondingly modest.

After the separation, operating leverage is lower and more symmetrical. The swing will come from Machinery volume rather than plant absorption. The central cost block also becomes more visible, because spreading it over €1 billion rather than €2 billion of revenue makes it worth 2.4 points of margin rather than 1.3 points today.

Financial leverage turns from a drag into a support within 18 months, and the size of the support depends on a capital-allocation decision. Net interest of €29.7 million in FY2025 was about 17% of adjusted pre-tax profit, so a 10% move in EBIT moved EPS by about 12%. Net interest had tripled from €7.8 million in FY2021, because TKH funded its capital-spending programme with debt. The model takes covenant net debt to about €440 million at end-2026 (1.5x EBITDA) and then to about €340 million of net cash at end-2027, after the sale and a first €50 million buyback. The interest swing alone is worth about €0.55 of EPS on today's share count. TKH moves from the most geared company in its peer set (Nexans at 0.4x, NKT in net cash, Basler and Jenoptik with little debt) to the least geared.

Pricing power is real where TKH is the only qualified supplier and absent where it is one of several. In Machinery, TKH uses pricing power through product mix rather than list prices.

Evidence for pricing power

  • Machinery earned a record 19.4% return on sales in FY2025 on an 8.6% volume decline, and 16.0% in H1 2026 on a 5.7% decline: TKH did not give price back
  • Launch customers accepted UNIXX pricing
  • Subsea contracts were signed at scarcity terms with escalation clauses
  • The onshore frameworks reprice an eight-year order book at post-shortage terms

Evidence against

  • Vision's added-value margin stayed flat at 62.7% through a restock: held, not raised
  • An industry expert reports negligible price differences among cable makers
  • Electrification's 8% margin shows that scarcity pricing has not yet reached the profit line

For the model, price adds roughly the inflation rate to continuing revenue, plus about one point of Automation margin over four years from UNIXX and the software share of sales. Standalone software licensing has been announced but has no disclosed revenue; it is unmodelled upside worth about 0.6 points of Automation margin for every €10 million of licence revenue.

Cost-out is real but small next to the perimeter change, and stranded costs arrive first. The identifiable saving in the continuing business is €10 to €15 million a year by FY2029, from bringing central costs down to Smiths' ratio of 1.5% of revenue. Vision site and purchasing synergies could add perhaps €5 million, although European wage inflation has consistently absorbed such savings at TKH. Cable plant fixed costs cannot be cut without losing capacity, and research spending at 5% of sales should not be cut. One-off costs come first: about €20 million in FY2026, €35 million in FY2027 and €10 million in FY2028. The working-capital release is mostly a perimeter effect: the group's working-capital ratio falls from 18.3% to about 12.5% at separation without anyone doing anything, and the released working capital leaves inside the sold business and is paid for in the sale price.

Feedback loops: two genuine reinforcing loops lie ahead, and both depend on a decision or event that has not yet happened.

LoopTypeHow it works and when
Capital allocationreinforcingThe sale proceeds reduce the share count, which lifts EPS, which lifts the share price at which the next buyback tranche is bought. Starts only if TKH decides to return the cash.
Tyre-machine replacementreinforcingDeferral builds a larger replacement wave rather than destroying demand, as in 2023, when Smart Manufacturing grew 17% once component shortages cleared. Starts when tyre makers release orders.
Eemshaven absorption and the Vision restockone-time repairLook like loops but are one-time repairs, mostly complete by mid-2027.
Peer cable capacity from Q2 2027balancingCaps the Electrification sale multiple. Arrives after the base-case closing, so the buyer bears it.
Chinese 2D vision pricingbalancingCaps the Vision margin, which is why the model holds Vision's margin at 21% from FY2028.

Inference and so-what. At TKH, revenue growth produces outsized profit growth. But the largest fixed-cost block, Eemshaven, is being sold at the point where it fills up, so the outsized part of the next two years' profit growth belongs to the buyer. The shareholder keeps a moderately levered product business plus a balance-sheet swing worth about €0.55 of EPS on its own and up to €0.90 more through the share count by FY2030.

Strongest counter-case. Operating leverage works in both directions. A slipped offshore call-off could leave Eemshaven under-used again before closing. Machinery's margin floor of 14% to 15% sits below the model's 15.0% for FY2027 if intake stays near €50 million a quarter; one downside-scenario report in the research file sizes Automation EBITA down over 25% in that case. Stranded costs could run at €30 million rather than €24 million.

What would change my view. Upward: disclosed licence revenue; a central-cost target from Grandi below Smiths' ratio. Downward: Vision's added-value margin falling below 61%; a working-capital spike that takes leverage back toward 2.0x before closing and blocks the buyback authorisation.

Market versus me. The market models operating leverage on the consolidated perimeter (consensus FY2028 EBITDA margin of 17.6% against 13.2% in FY2025) and does not model the balance-sheet swing or the share count at all. Viewforth models both, and treats the consolidated operating leverage as the buyer's from mid-2027.

Score: 60. Operating leverage of about 50% drop-through and a financial-leverage swing from 1.8x to net cash put TKH above the European median on this topic; the deductions are that the biggest fixed-cost lever is being sold, pricing power is mix-based, and cost-out is small next to the perimeter effect.

Two cautions apply when reading the model's own numbers.

  1. The model's FY2027 free cash flow of €339.5 million is a mechanical artefact. The model books the €260 million of working capital that leaves inside the sold businesses as a cash release, and omits about €35 million of separation cash costs. The Analyst's €49 million is the economic figure, and cumulative free cash flow over the four years is about €380 million, not €680 million.
  2. The model buys back shares at about today's price, while the model's own return table has the share price at €76 by December 2027. The model's FY2028 to FY2030 EPS therefore run 5% to 9% above an internally consistent series; the Analyst's cross-check gives about €3.37, €4.12 and €4.85. This memo uses the model's figures as the forecasts of record and treats FY2029 and FY2030 as the upper edge of the range.

Is there scope for double-digit growth and higher margins than in the past?

MeasureVerdictReasoning
Revenue growthNo, not durablyFY2026's 11% is a repair from a low base plus metal-price pass-through. The continuing business grows 7% to 9% including acquisitions and 5% to 6% organically, which is the company's own target band.
EPS growthYes, emphaticallyFrom the FY2027 trough, EPS grows 43% in FY2028, 26% in FY2029 and 21% in FY2030 on the model, and about 25% a year compounded on the cross-check. Roughly a third comes from operations, a third from the share count, and a third from the first full year of net cash and lower one-off costs.
MarginsHigher than any year in the decadeThe continuing business's 18% to 20.7% EBITDA margin is ordinary against the peer set it joins (Basler, Jenoptik and Cognex at 20% to 29%, with net cash) and extraordinary against its own history (13% to 15%). The rise comes by construction.
Cash conversionMuch betterFrom 0.3x to 0.7x of net income in the last three years to 75% to 80% of adjusted net profit from FY2028, because the business stops funding milestone-phased cable projects and a plant.

Against consensus, the model is ahead in FY2026 and on a different perimeter after that.

  • FY2026: the model's EBITDA is 2% below consensus (€296 million against €302 million), but EPS is 13% above on the model's basis and 3% above on the company's basis (€3.19 against €3.10). The gap comes from interest and tax charges that brokers carry too high.
  • FY2027: on the consolidated perimeter the model reproduces consensus (EBIT about €219 million, EPS €3.71) with a different composition. On the continuing perimeter the published series is not comparable and will be re-based.
  • FY2028 and FY2029: the published medians (€4.28 and €5.52) are on the wrong perimeter and will not survive the signing. The relevant comparison is the model's €3.51 and €4.43, on 34 million and 31 million shares.

Against the past four to six years, the shape of the business changes. Revenue halves by construction and then grows at a rate similar to the last six years' 2.8% compound plus acquisitions, but with a different mix of drivers: customer design cycles, machine replacement and restocking, rather than cable-project call-offs and copper prices. The margin band narrows from 10% to 13%, with swings driven by plant absorption, to 16% to 19%, with swings driven by Machinery volume. EPS falls in the year of separation and then compounds faster than in any period since 2021 to 2022. Net debt disappears for two years and returns modestly as buybacks and bolt-on acquisitions exceed cash generation.

Strongest counter-case. In the one-third probability case in which the separation slips past 2027 or fails, FY2027 revenue is about €2,047 million, adjusted EPS about €3.71, and FY2028 EPS about €4.10 on the consolidated perimeter as Electrification approaches a 19% EBITDA margin. That case is better for reported FY2027 and FY2028 EPS than the base case, but worse for the multiple, the share count and the four-year path, and it is the case consensus currently publishes.

What would change my view. Two consecutive quarters of Machinery intake below €60 million would lead Viewforth to cut FY2028 Machinery revenue by 10% and group EPS by about 6%. A sale price above €1.0 billion, returned through the buyback, would lift FY2029 EPS by about €0.25. A change in research-capitalisation policy would cut the standalone margin by 2 points, without a cash effect.

Market versus me. Consensus is credible for FY2026, demanding but achievable for a consolidated FY2027, and unusable as a group series after that: the market has not begun to model the business the shareholder will own. As far as the files show, the model's continuing-perimeter series is the only one in existence.

Score: 58. Double-digit EPS growth from FY2028 and margins above the decade's range are better than the European median; the deductions are that revenue growth is mid-single-digit, the improvement is mostly by construction, and the four-year numbers rest on a sale price and a capital-return decision not yet taken.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over the next 6 to 12 months

Key message. The screens will read worst in the first half of 2027 for reasons of accounting perimeter, not value. The genuine upgrade scope arrives from mid-2027, and the capital return is the largest unmodelled item.

The sequence of events, and what each event is likely to do to estimates.

WhenEventWhat to expect
About 10 Nov 2026Q3 trading updateFY2026 guidance reiterated (about 85% probability). The Smart Manufacturing consensus revenue line (€457 million) is the most likely to be cut: about 60% probability of a 3% to 5% segment cut, worth 1% to 2% of group EPS, offset by Electrification. Net FY2027 EPS revision after November of minus 2% to plus 2%, with upgrades and downgrades roughly balanced for the first time in a year. The readable tests are the Machinery order book against €259.2 million and whether "temporary deferral" becomes "extended".
March 2027FY2026 results, Grandi's firstFY2026 guidance beaten by about 30% on EBITA (above 90% probability). FY2026 consensus EPS drifts up 2% to 4% across the two events, led by ING catching up (ING's €2.41 appears to sit on a different basis) and by lower financial charges. Then the reset: the restated margin target, one-off costs, and a dividend of €1.60 against €1.70.
Q1 or Q2 2027, the quarter after signingThe IFRS 5 re-basing windowElectrification and Other move into discontinued operations for the whole of FY2027, with restated comparatives. Brokers move FY2027 revenue from about €2,060 million to about €1,030 million, EBITDA from €343 million to about €185 million, and EPS from €3.71 to about €2.1 to €2.5 before a disposal gain of roughly €7.50 a share that some brokers will leave in reported EPS and others will strip out. Precedents (Sandvik, Smiths, DSM-Firmenich, Aalberts) say consensus will be "fragmented and messy" for at least a quarter. The first standalone half-year (August 2027) is a modest downgrade risk. The capital-allocation announcement is the largest upgrade driver in euros: each €200 million of buyback adds about 5% to 6% to FY2029 EPS and appears in nobody's numbers. Machinery is two-sided.

The sell-side's threshold of €80 million of quarterly Machinery intake is a construct traced back to TKH's 2011 results, and TKH reports order books only at half-years, so quarterly intake cannot be read directly.

The gaps between Viewforth and consensus, line by line.

  • FY2026 EPS: Viewforth's €3.19 against consensus €3.10, a favourable gap.
  • FY2027 consolidated EPS: level with consensus, with a different composition and a negative tilt in November.
  • FY2028 and FY2029 on the re-based series: by end-2027, about 55% probability of upgrades, 30% of no change and 15% of downgrades. The two drivers that would lift estimates, the buyback and the Machinery turn, are a decision and a cycle that brokers will not model until announced or visible, and a conservative first guide leaves room.
  • Dividend: a dividend held at €1.60 for FY2027, against a €1.98 consensus, will register as a cut to expectations at the March 2028 results unless TKH re-bases its dividend policy to cash flow. Nobody has flagged the gap.
  • Target prices: Jefferies, whose numbers lead consensus, builds its €65 target on 12.2x EBITDA for Electrification. A sale near Viewforth's €850 million would see the Jefferies target fall, while the other brokers' targets (€57 to €62) hold.

The narrative: the market's story covers the break-up and leaves out the aftermath.

The standalone Automation story has no narrative beyond the 2028 targets and cannot acquire one before August 2027.

Inference and so-what. The next six months are neutral to unfavourable for upgrades, because the only unpriced positives in that window are a sale price or a return framework above expectations. Months six to eighteen are favourable: the re-based consensus starts low, the first standalone half-year shows a business earning a 16% to 17% margin with net cash, and the capital return is the largest unmodelled item. Revision breadth, the consensus series and headline EPS will all give false negative readings in the first half of 2027. The market's narrative will be most out of line with Viewforth's assessment, in Viewforth's favour, in the quarter when the screens say estimates have been cut by 40%.

Strongest counter-case. The shares have already paid for the event: the forward multiple is at the 84th percentile of five years and the price is 16% above its 200-day average. The unpriced items that arrive first are negatives. One research report in the file puts the temporary dislocation on the re-basing at 15% to 20%; Viewforth would put it at 5% to 10%, because the free float has followed the break-up for a year. Even 5% to 10% is a real cost for a holder judged on the next two quarters.

What would change my view. Upward: a return framework or first buyback tranche at the March results (about 35% probability; Arcadis launched a 5% buyback on its new chief financial officer's first day). Downward: Grandi's first guide set on a segment basis without a central-cost figure, which would leave the "16% against 17% to 19%" margin surprise for August 2027.

Score: 55. Substantial, un-modelled upgrade scope on the right perimeter from mid-2027 is offset by a scheduled six-month window in which guidance, consensus and the narrative all read worse before they read better; favourable on an 18-month view, unfavourable on a six-month one, so mid-table.

#8 Current momentum in guidance, estimates, narrative and share price, and the same for key peers

Key message. Momentum is strong on every measure the dashboard pins, but it sits on a consolidated earnings series that will be re-based in 2027, so the measured momentum will reverse mechanically for a quarter.

TKH's share-price momentum is strong, with the first sign of consolidation. The dashboard grades technical momentum A (18 October). The price was €50.95 on 21 October, within a 52-week range of €33.64 to €55.25, and 16.3% above a 200-day average (€43.80) that has risen in every one of the last twelve months. The price has now slipped below its 50-day average (€51.93), so the first leg of a consolidation has begun.

Sell-side earnings momentum is graded B (17 October), with nothing moved in the last month. The last month's lull is typical before a Q3 update. The revision-momentum score is 10.

Change in consensus3 months6 months12 months

Guidance momentum is flat, and narrative momentum is strong. TKH has reiterated its guidance floor, raised its Electrification standalone targets in August, and given no numerical group guide. The break-up cohort of diversified industrial groups is the one part of the sector the market has paid for (up 45% over twelve months), and the sector digest names TKH as value that does not need a re-rating, because the carve-out is worth over half of the market capitalisation.

Peers: three groups matter, and they point in different directions

The break-up cohort shows that outcomes separate on execution. Inside the dashboard sector, the break-up names have led, and the two that disappointed on execution, Volati and Smiths, sit at the bottom (Smiths also carries a sell-side momentum grade of F). "Break-up" is therefore not a single trade. thyssenkrupp's tk accelis unit lists on 28 October, with Deutsche Bank's equity value range at €1.2 to €3.3 billion. TKH's daily returns have a correlation of 0.44 and an R-squared of 19% with the peer basket over the latest six months (0.51 with Aalberts), so about four-fifths of TKH's share-price variance is its own: on the basket measured, TKH's multiple is company-driven.

The cable makers set Electrification's value, and that channel has been running against TKH for four months without showing in TKH's price. The market reads across from the cable makers, which are not in the peer basket. Their shares have fallen about a fifth from their June peaks and the sector's P/E has de-rated by about 30%.

The vision peers that will matter after the sale have strong momentum. Jenoptik raised its guidance, Basler guides €270 to €290 million of revenue after a book-to-bill of 1.30x, Cognex reported record revenue, Keyence earns a 54% operating margin, and Teledyne reported a record Q3 beat and raised its guidance.

The tyre makers that set Machinery's demand do not. Michelin is flat and Goodyear is cutting; Continental and Pirelli are expanding, but with construction starting only from 2027.

Inference and so-what. Momentum is strong on every measure the dashboard pins, is a year old, and is broad across target prices and ratings, with laggard brokers (ING, KBC) still to catch up with Jefferies. The momentum supports the price into the separation announcement. The momentum is also the reason the entry price is not cheap against TKH's own history: the 24-month-forward P/E of 12.05x on consensus sits at the 84th percentile of five years (median 10.4x) but only the 52nd percentile of ten years, because the shares traded at 14x to 17x from 2016 to 2021. This memo uses the ten-year window to set the fair multiple and the five-year window to judge the entry price.

Strongest counter-case. TKH is a crowded holding at the 87th relative-strength percentile, in a market regime with Fragility at Double Underweight. With only €5 million of daily traded value, 2x leverage until closing, and a dated catalyst that needs financing, TKH could become a source of liquidity in a risk-off market. A weak tk accelis debut, or an execution warning from NKT or Prysmian, would hit TKH's sum of the parts before TKH reports anything.

What would change my view. Upward: the price reclaiming its 50-day average after the November update; positive FY2027 EPS revisions in November despite a Machinery cut. Downward: a further 10% fall in cable-sector shares before signing; HAL reducing its stake.

Market versus me. The market and Viewforth agree that the momentum is real and earned. The difference is that the market's momentum sits on the consolidated series that will be re-based: the dashboard's B for sell-side momentum will print as a D or F for a quarter in 2027 without any change in value, and Richard should discount that reading in advance.

Score: 70. Technical momentum A, sell-side momentum B, an 88% buy share and a cohort in favour put TKH in the top quarter of European companies on momentum now; the deduction is for the unmeasured cable-peer channel running against it and for a six-month window in which the measured momentum will mechanically reverse.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Key message. The mechanism is simple (sell the worse half, keep the better half, return the cash), but the reporting of it will be the most complicated in TKH's history, and the risks in the chain multiply rather than add. The forecasts are more fragile to two external events than TKH's history was, and more robust to management error. All the sudden risks are dated and trackable.

The case has one event, one cycle and one decision. The event is the sale, the cycle is tyre makers' capital spending, and the decision is the use of the proceeds. Together they supply about two-thirds of the four-year EPS growth and almost all of the change in margin, cash and balance sheet. The drivers of FY2020 to FY2025 (cable projects, the Eemshaven ramp-up, metal prices and a destock) were also few, but they were operational and inside the company, and management controlled them badly. The next four years' drivers are a transaction in a financing environment the company does not control, a customer capital-spending cycle it does not control, and a capital-allocation decision it does control.

The chain from sale to re-rating is sequential, so its risks multiply. What must happen first, in order of time:

  1. The transaction in Q1 2027 at a price the market accepts. TKH has never done a deal of this size.
  2. Control of stranded costs through 2027. TKH has never run a lean head office, and the shareholder circular itself warns of duplication.
  3. The capital-return decision at the first capital markets day. TKH's record is one €25 million buyback in 2022 and nothing since.

About three-quarters of FY2029 EPS rests on strengths TKH has already demonstrated: segment margins held through a trough, VMI's franchise, Eemshaven's repair, on-time disposals, and lower interest once debt falls. A quarter of FY2029 EPS, and the whole of the re-rating, rests on strengths TKH would still have to acquire.

Segment profit is predictable; the path from segment profit to EPS is not. The company's targets fix continuing segment operating profit to within about 10%. Between segment EBITA and EPS, however, sit four variables the company does not guide, shown in the figure below. The company's incentive metrics omit EPS, so nothing inside the company pulls those four variables toward a target number.

The range of outcomes is narrow for five months and then splits into two branches. For FY2026 the range is narrow: adjusted EBITA of €248 million plus or minus 5%, and EPS of €3.05 to €3.35 on the company's basis. For the thirteen months after that the range is wide. FY2027 reported EPS will be either about €3.7 (consolidated) or about €2.1 to €2.5 plus a €7.50 disposal gain (continuing), and the two branches do not overlap; which branch applies depends on the signing date. Operations alone, on either perimeter, give a range of about plus or minus 8% on EBITA, which is narrow for a short-cycle industrial company. The extra width comes from the perimeter, the sale price, the one-off costs and the capital-return decision.

The sudden risks are all dated inside the next twelve months and all trackable; the slow risk sets the FY2028 number. The risks that could hit the share price suddenly are a slipped sale, a cable-sector de-rating, a Grandi reset, the IFRS 5 optics, a reversal of the break-up cohort like Volati's, and a weak tk accelis debut. The slow and untrackable risk is Tier 1 tyre makers' capital spending. TKH's disclosure is adequate for the operations (half-year order books and colour in trading updates) but poor for the two things that decide the next six months: the transaction, about which TKH will say nothing until signing, and the standalone cost base, which will stay invisible until March 2027 at the earliest and probably August 2027.

Monitoring sheet: five dated readings

  1. November 2026: the order-book figures in the Q3 update
  2. The signing announcement
  3. March 2027: one-off costs and the central-cost disclosure
  4. March 2027: the dividend and the form of guidance
  5. February 2027: tyre makers' capital-spending guides

External monitors, more informative than TKH's own disclosure

  • Machinery: Michelin, Goodyear, Bridgestone, Continental, Pirelli
  • Vision: Cognex, Basler, Jenoptik, the VDMA (German machinery association) series
  • Sale price: Prysmian, NKT, Nexans, progress at Karlskrona, offshore developers' final investment decisions, tk accelis

Sudden fundamental risks over 18 months: the plant and the sale are the same bet. The table below sizes each risk. The joint risk that matters most is Eemshaven and the sale together, because a plant failure would collapse the sale value. The research house's spring estimate of a 48% chance that both succeed has risen to perhaps 60% to 65%, now that the plant ramp-up half of the bet has been delivered.

The downside to a fair trough multiple is 35% to 45%, cushioned by the sum of the parts. The five-year 25th percentile of the forward multiple is 9.4x and the 10th percentile 8.9x; the ten-year "crash" band is 9.5x. On consensus FY2027 EPS of €3.71, multiples of 8.5x to 9.5x give €32 to €35; a cut EPS of €3.20 at 9x gives €29. Other reference points cluster nearby: Jefferies' bear-case value of €30, the floor of €25 to €30 in the research file's risk report, the December 2024 capitulation low of €30, and the 52-week low of €33.64. The sum of the parts cushions the fall: Nexans' 7x multiple on €125 million of Electrification EBITDA, plus the rest of the group at today's 7.7x EV/EBITDA, puts the trough nearer the mid-€30s than the high €20s.

Viewforth's 18-month price range from €50.25.

CaseProbabilityPrice, December 2027What it requires
Upsideabout 25%€72 to €78A sale at €1.0 billion or more, a stabilised Machinery order book, and a return framework of €300 million or more
Baseabout 50%€60 to €66The model's base case, with the multiple at about 14.4x
Downsideabout 25%€36 to €40A sale slipping into late 2027, or a listing at Nexans' multiple, with Machinery intake below €60 million a quarter through mid-2027

Precedents favour TKH on its own history and split on separations. TKH's own history shows two kinds of task. In the 2021 to 2022 short-cycle upturn, when TKH was cheap and geared and had cut costs, EPS tripled in two years. In the 2023 to 2025 capital-intensive ramp-up, ROCE fell from 19.8% to 13.8%, EPS fell from €4.26 to €2.62, and guidance was missed twice. The next three years are the first kind of task.

Separations that went well

  • thyssenkrupp: combined value up 15% on the TKMS debut
  • Smiths: continuing operations beat guidance in 2023 (organic growth 13.5%, operating profit up 27%)

Separations that went badly

  • Aalberts: EPS cut 11% to 13% for 13% of revenue removed
  • Sandvik Machining: valued at 4x EBITA for a period
  • Norma: shares down 15% on signing, with the remaining core at a 0% to 1% margin
  • Volati: down 76%

The precedents are European mid-caps that sold or distributed 35% to 45% of revenue. The variable that separated the good outcomes from the bad was whether the remaining core business was in an upcycle when the transaction closed. For TKH the answer is half yes (Vision) and half not yet (Machinery), which is why the base case carries 50% probability rather than more. In the sell-side's own survey, sum-of-the-parts calls realise in under 30% of cases within two years; TKH's trigger is dated but not yet priced.

Market versus me. The market treats the case as a simple event trade. Viewforth treats the case as a simple mechanism wrapped in the most complicated eighteen months of reporting the company will ever produce, and sees that complexity as the source of the opportunity.

Score: 40. A sequential, transaction-dependent chain, four un-guided variables between segment profit and EPS, a reporting discontinuity inside the horizon and a 35% to 45% downside to a trough multiple put TKH in the riskier half of European companies; the credits are that the operations are predictable, the risks are dated and trackable, and the earnings skew is positive.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Key message. Two lifecycles are running at once, out of phase. The break-up event is Reinforcing; the standalone automation story is only Bottoming to Turning Up. The hand-over between them during 2027 will look like a stall on the screens at exactly the point where the second lifecycle's upside is largest and least priced.

The dashboard's rule gives a starting phase of Reinforcing. The rule rests on a two-year-forward P/E of 12.56x, a 200-day average that has risen in every month of the last twelve, a year-old upgrade cycle and a cohort in favour.

The event narrative is Reinforcing, with one or two steps left. The event narrative is "a break-up with a date, and a carve-out worth over half the market value". The deep estimate cuts of 2024 are two years behind. The shares bottomed at €30 in December 2024, turned up on the September 2025 break-up announcement, broadened on the 2026 earnings beats and the August standalone targets, and are now reinforcing on the extraordinary general meeting, the chief executive appointment and unanimous sell-side support. The signing and the proceeds are the remaining steps before the event lifecycle is complete.

The standalone narrative is Bottoming to Turning Up. The standalone narrative is "a focused automation leader with a cash pile". No broker has published continuing-perimeter estimates, the standalone margin after central costs has never been in print, no capital-return policy exists, and the chief executive who will own the story has not spoken.

The hand-over contains a scheduled stall. The share price will move from the first lifecycle to the second during 2027. In the re-basing quarter, every momentum reading the dashboard pins (sell-side momentum, the revision score and the consensus series) will say Stalling or Collapsing while the value of the company is unchanged.

Evidence that Reinforcing is the right reading today

  • Estimates have risen for a year and laggard brokers still have to catch up
  • The sequence of dated developments over 18 months is unusually full: the November update, signing, Grandi's arrival, tk accelis, the March results, closing, the buyback, a capital markets day, and the first standalone half-year
  • The drivers of the next two steps are new and unmodelled

Evidence that the reading is fragile

  • The multiple is at the 84th percentile of five years
  • The unpriced items that arrive first are negatives
  • Once complete, the event lifecycle hands over to a narrative that does not yet exist

Inference and so-what. The stock is Reinforcing on the event, faces a scheduled apparent stall in H1 2027, and should then be Turning Up on the standalone business from August 2027 if the first standalone numbers are good. The practical consequence is that the stock will look as if it is Stalling at precisely the point where the second lifecycle's upside is largest and least priced. Richard should decide in advance how he will read the screens in that quarter.

Strongest counter-case. If the sale slips or is priced at a listing-route multiple, the event lifecycle moves from Reinforcing to Stalling with no second lifecycle to hand over to. The stock then reverts to the consolidated series on a cheaper multiple, with the conglomerate discount intact.

What would change my view. A sale signed above €1.0 billion together with a return framework would move both lifecycles to Reinforcing at once and remove the stall. A slip would move the event lifecycle to Stalling.

Market versus me. The market sees one lifecycle at Reinforcing. Viewforth sees two, with the hand-over between them inside the investment horizon.

Score: 58. Reinforcing on the dashboard's rule and on the event, which is better than the European median, with the deduction that the next lifecycle has not started and the hand-over will read as a stall.

#11 The fair multiple

Key message. Viewforth accepts the guideline 16.41x as the fair multiple in the delivery case, but expects about 14x by December 2027. On continuing earnings the market already pays 14.3x, so much of the apparent re-rating is a re-labelling; the genuine re-rating closes only when TKH shows standalone numbers.

The guideline is 16.41x, 31% above today's 12.56x. Viewforth's rule sets the fair multiple from the lifecycle phase and the stock's ten-year range; for the Reinforcing phase it is the 90th percentile, 16.41x two-year-forward earnings. The ten-year range, excluding outliers, runs from 9.5x at the 10th percentile through a median of 12.5x and a 75th percentile of 14.4x to 16.4x at the 90th. The stock reached 16x or more four times in the decade (October 2017, May 2018 at 16.7x, December 2019 and November 2020), each time during an upturn in its product businesses with no capital project under way. The stock fell to 8.5x to 9x in 2022 to 2024, as the cable plant ramp-up consumed capital.

Viewforth accepts 16.41x for the Reinforcing phase in a peak-delivery window, on three conditions. By the time the multiple is applied, three things must be in print: a signed sale at or above Viewforth's base price, a capital-return framework, and a first standalone half-year showing 16% to 17% margins with net cash. Those three disclosures turn the stock from a conglomerate at its historical peak multiple into a standalone automation company at a multiple that its new peer set would regard as modest (Basler trades at about 20x forward earnings, Jenoptik at about 25x, and Cognex and Keyence higher).

Three arguments for 16.41x or more

  • The business that remains has earned a 27% pro forma ROCE and 18% to 21% segment margins through a destock; the decade of 10% to 13% group margins that produced the ten-year range never did
  • The balance sheet moves from the most geared in its peer set to net cash
  • Jefferies' sum-of-the-parts multiples for Vision and Machinery (16.6x and 14.5x EV/EBITDA) translate to a P/E well above 16x

Three arguments that hold it at 16.41x rather than higher

  • The STAK structure caps the takeover premium that a €1 billion automation pure-play would otherwise attract
  • Machinery is cyclical and 2D vision is commoditising, so the standalone earnings are not those of a quality compounder
  • The chief executive, the earnings base and the reporting basis all change inside the horizon, so the forecasts are more uncertain than a peak-delivery phase implies

Read correctly, the multiple the market pays today is already defendable.

  • On consensus consolidated earnings: 12.56x.
  • On the model's continuing-perimeter FY2028 EPS of €3.51: 14.3x, inside the "defendable" band.
  • On an enterprise basis: a market capitalisation of about €2.0 billion, plus €0.5 billion of covenant net debt, less about €0.95 billion of proceeds, leaves about €1.55 billion for Automation. That is about 8.4x Automation's FY2027 EBITDA of €185 million and 9.5x its EBITA, against 13x to 16x for vision and machinery peers.

The move from 12.56x to 16.41x on the two-year-forward P/E is therefore partly a re-labelling, because the market already pays a defendable multiple for the continuing business, and partly a genuine discount to the peer set that will close only when TKH shows standalone numbers.

Probability-weighted multiple for December 2027ProbabilityMultipleReasoning

Strongest counter-case. The ten-year 90th percentile was set between 2017 and 2020 by a conglomerate whose consolidated earnings included cables. Applying that multiple to a smaller, more cyclical standalone business, in a market that refuses re-ratings, is a stretch, and 14.4x is the honest ceiling until August 2027.

What would change my view. A return framework of €300 million or more at the March results would move Viewforth's base multiple to 16x. A sale at a listing-route multiple with no return framework would cap the multiple at 12.5x.

Market versus me. The sell-side's targets (€57 to €68) imply 13x to 15x the re-based FY2028 EPS. The guideline sits above the sell-side; Viewforth's expected multiple sits between the two, with the guideline as the delivery-case multiple.

Score: 55. A guideline of 16.41x is well-founded on the stock's own history and the quality of the business that remains, and I accept it for the delivery case; the deduction is that it depends on three disclosures none of which exists yet, so the expected multiple over the next 12 months is nearer 14x.

#12 Total shareholder return, by the DuPont split

Key message. The delivery case returns about 57% to December 2027 including dividends, about a third from earnings and two-thirds from the multiple. Viewforth's probability-weighted expectation is about 25% (about 20% annualised), with outcomes positively skewed in size (plus 45% against minus 25%) and symmetric in probability.

The model's return at the guideline multiple. From €50.25 on 22 October 2026, the model's template shows:

Two reading notes on the template. First, in both columns the stated return equals the change in the share price (€75.94 and €98.38 against €50.25). The template's dividend component sits inside its split rather than on top, so this memo treats the declared dividends as additional. Second, the template's split is an artefact of the FY2027 perimeter change. The template reads the model's "two-year-forward P/E today" of 16.9x (today's price divided by a blend of continuing-perimeter FY2027 EPS of €2.45 and FY2028 EPS of €3.51), and interprets the fall in published EPS as a de-rating plus an earnings collapse that then reverses. The split should not be quoted as a decomposition.

The economic decomposition of the 18-month return: earnings are the engine and the multiple is the amplifier. The starting point is what the market pays today: 12.56x on about €4.00 of two-year-forward consolidated consensus EPS. The end point is what the model pays in December 2027: 16.41x on about €4.63 of two-year-forward continuing EPS (€75.94 divided by 16.41).

  • Earnings rise 16%, from €4.00 to €4.63. On a like-for-like basis, the interest saving, the buyback and Machinery's recovery replace the lost Electrification earnings, so that FY2029 continuing EPS (€4.43) roughly matches FY2028 consolidated consensus (€4.28), with growth on top.
  • The multiple rises 31%, from 12.56x to 16.41x.
  • The product of the two is the model's 51% price gain, and dividends add about 6% more, for a total return of about 57%.

About a third of the price gain comes from earnings and about two-thirds from the multiple. The earnings compounding from the FY2027 trough is what justifies the multiple.

Piece of the returnWhat it rests onSkew and exposure
Earnings, +16%Three-quarters on demonstrated strengths (segment margins, VMI's franchise, Eemshaven's repair, falling interest); a quarter on strengths to be acquired (central-cost discipline, the capital return, a transaction of this size)positive FY2026 is a floor, and the buyback and the replacement wave appear in no published number
