The three-year figure is overstated; quote about 70% with dividends. The template's €98.38 is 16.41x about €6.00 of two-year-forward EPS at June 2029. That EPS is above any year the model holds (FY2030 is €5.35) and rests on growth extrapolated beyond FY2030 and on the model's buyback mechanic. On the Analyst's cross-check (FY2030 EPS of €4.85), the three-year value is nearer €80 to €85 at the guideline multiple: a price gain of 60% to 70%, or about 70% to 80% with dividends, rather than 96%. This memo quotes the three-year return as "about 70% at the guideline multiple with dividends" and the 18-month return as "about 55% in the delivery case with dividends".

Viewforth's probability-weighted return is about 25%. Using the price range in #9 (25% probability of €72 to €78, 50% of €60 to €66, 25% of €36 to €40), the expected December 2027 price is about €60. Adding €3.20 of dividends gives a total return of about 25% over 14 months, or about 20% annualised. The dispersion is wide in both directions and the bad news comes first. The delivery case (the model's 51% price gain) is a 25% to 30% probability outcome on its own and the top of the 50% probability base case. The skew in outcomes is positive in size (plus 45% against minus 25%) and symmetric in probability.

Strongest counter-case. If the market holds the multiple at 12.56x and earnings land as modelled, the 18-month return is about 22% including dividends. If the sale slips and the multiple falls to 10.5x on a cut consolidated series, the return is about minus 20%. The return at the guideline multiple is therefore a statement of what the stock is worth if every step in the sequence lands, not a forecast.

What would change my view. A signing above €1.0 billion together with a return framework would move Viewforth's expected return toward the model's; a slip would halve the expected return.

Market versus me. Sell-side targets of €57 to €68 imply 13% to 35% price upside. The model at the guideline multiple sits above the sell-side range; Viewforth's expectation sits inside the range, with the model's figure as the delivery case.

Score: 62. A 51% delivery-case price gain in 14 months, plus dividends, two-thirds of it from a multiple that has a well-founded path to being earned and a third from earnings that are positively skewed, is well above the European median; the deductions are the dependence on a transaction and a chief executive not yet seen and a probability-weighted return nearer 25%.

#13 Summary conclusion

TKH is a well-dated, well-founded break-up whose first half the market has fully priced and whose second half nobody has modelled. What leaves (an 8% margin, working capital at 25.6% of sales, and a repaired plant whose scarcity window closes in 2027) is worse than what stays (an 18% margin, working capital at 12.4%, a tyre-building fortress and a contested but profitable vision specialist). The proceeds, nearly half the market capitalisation, convert 1.8x leverage into net cash with €600 million to return.

Earnings are the engine. The model's forecasts, which this memo does not change, have EPS falling 30% in the year of separation by construction and then compounding at about 25% a year through FY2030, a third of it through the lower share count.

The multiple is the swing factor. On the model's forecasts the shares are worth €75.94 by December 2027 at the guideline 16.41x, a 51% price gain in the delivery case, with dividends on top. Viewforth's probability-weighted total return is about 25%, because the multiple is the largest swing item and will be earned only when standalone numbers that do not yet exist are in print.

The sequence is the steer. The next six months carry the negatives: a reset, a restated target, a dividend below consensus, and a re-basing that prints as a 40% cut. The following twelve months carry the positives: closing, proceeds, the return framework, the first standalone half-year and a late-2027 Machinery turn.

The risks that matter are external. The two risks that can break the case, the sale price in a hostile financing environment and the tyre makers' capital-spending cycle, are outside management's control. The operating businesses that remain have shown they hold margin through a trough. The case is therefore robust to the thing TKH has historically done badly, and fragile to two things TKH has never had to do.

The action. The best entry point of the next 18 months is likely to be inside the window in which the screens say estimates have been cut by 40% while the value of the company has not changed.

B

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: B. A shareholder-approved separation with a target quarter, an external chief executive with a start date, reset targets, completed capex and an authorised buyback, backed by structural grid and offshore demand and a vision restock, are strong, dated and broad change forces. They are held out of the A band because two of the three external tailwinds attach to the asset being sold and the internal forces hinge on one transaction.

C

Foundations' Robustness: C. A genuine fortress in VMI and a defensible 3D vision niche sit alongside a commoditising 2D business, a decade of 10% to 13% group margins, poor cash conversion, an earnings base needing four corrections, a management team that is the weakest element and is changing, and a STAK governance structure that travels with the new company.

C

Setups' Fit/Crispness: C. In substance the case is a Big Corporate Change-driven EPSU setup: a break-up that converts a geared conglomerate into a net-cash automation company and lifts EPS through the share count and the interest line. The fit is not crisp, because the step-up arrives after a one-year trough, is routed through a capital-allocation decision not yet taken, and starts from an entry multiple that is no longer in the first quartile of its own history.

D

Case Riskiness: D. A sequential chain (sale, proceeds, buyback, EPS, re-rating) whose risks multiply, four un-guided variables between segment profit and EPS, a reporting discontinuity and a chief-executive change inside the horizon, a 35% to 45% downside to a trough multiple, and a dependence on two external events make this a complex case. Predictable operations and dated, trackable risks partly redeem it.
